title: The Fog Chamber

sources.where: Choudhuri Ch. 2.2 (radiative transfer, eqs. 2.2-2.19), 2.3 (LTE, Kirchhoff 2.26), 2.4 (grey atmosphere 2.62-2.70), 2.5-2.6 (Rosseland, Kramers 2.79, Thomson 2.85), 2.8 (photon diffusion), exercises 2.5, 2.7

intro: The ship's observation chamber is full of fog. How much starlight gets through depends on one number, the optical depth $\tau$, and on what the fog emits itself, the source function $S_\nu$. This is the language of every spectrum you will ever read, and every exam has multiple-choice questions on it.

blocks.html: For isotropic radiation: $F_ u=0$ (as much goes up as down), $U_ u=4\pi I_ u/c$ and $P_ u=U_ u/3$. Inside a star the field is almost isotropic; the tiny anisotropy carries the whole luminosity.

$I_\nu$ is surface brightness. Flux is "how much light lands on my detector"; intensity is "how bright does the surface look". Walk away from a street lamp: the flux drops as $d^{-2}$ but the lamp's surface looks just as bright, it only gets smaller. In vacuum $dI_\nu/ds=0$.

Read the solution as a tug of war: the background $I_ u(0)$ is extinguished by $e^{- au}$, and the medium "pulls" the intensity towards its own $S_ u$. Optically thick ($ au\gg1$): you see $I_ u o S_ u$, only the surface layer ($ au\lesssim1$), nothing behind. Optically thin ($ au\ll1$): $I_ u\approx I_ u(0)+S_ u au_ u$, every atom along the line of sight contributes.

The opacity $\chi$ (per mass, m$^2$/kg) relates to the absorption coefficient by $\alpha=\chi\rho$. So $\tau=\int\chi\rho\,ds$: what matters is the column $\int\rho\,ds$, not the density or length separately.

Do not mix the thick/thin limits up: thick $\Rightarrow I\simeq S$ (independent of $\tau$); thin $\Rightarrow I\simeq S\tau$. And emission lines vs absorption lines: looking at a hot background through a cooler layer ($S<I(0)$) gives absorption lines; a hot thin gas against a dark sky gives emission lines.
HS24 winter MC4 (thick/thin limits), HS24 summer MC3 (two clouds, compare $\tau$), HS25 practice MC3 (an optically thick cloud can only be studied at its surface).

blocks.html: In full thermodynamic equilibrium four laws hold at one temperature $T$: Maxwell velocities, Boltzmann level populations $n_2/n_1\propto e^{-\Delta E/k_BT}$, Saha ionisation, and Planck radiation. A star is not in global equilibrium (it is hot inside, cool outside), but if particles and photons travel only a short distance (mean free path $l$) compared with the scale $L$ over which $T$ changes, each small region has its own well-defined $T$: local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE).
Kirchhoff says good absorbers are good emitters. If a gas in LTE absorbs strongly at a line frequency, it emits strongly there too, in exactly the ratio that would keep a blackbody field in balance.

Kirchhoff's law does not hold for scattering (Thomson scattering redirects photons, it does not thermally emit them). In the exam: "local but not global equilibrium" = variables depend on position and/or time AND $l\ll L$.

Saha equation (2.29): $\frac{x^2}{1-x}=\frac{(2\pi m_e)^{3/2}(k_BT)^{5/2}}{h^3P}e^{-\chi/k_BT}$. Plotting the ionised fraction $x$ against $T$ for hydrogen gives a steep S-curve whose position depends on density (pressure). At a stellar-photosphere density ($\rho\sim10^{-4}$ kg m$^{-3}$) hydrogen is half ionised at about $13\,500$ K, i.e. at $k_BT\approx\chi/11$, far below $\chi=13.6$ eV: there are so many more free states (phase space) than bound ones that ionisation wins long before typical photons carry 13.6 eV. (Checked numerically with (2.29); at the higher density of air, half ionisation needs ~$44\,000$ K.) The same argument explains why cosmic recombination happens at only ~3000 K.

check.q: A system of size $L$ with mean free path $l$ is in local but not global thermal equilibrium if $T$ and $P$

check.explain: Local: frequent collisions ($l\ll L$). Not global: gradients exist.

encounters.title: Stellar atmospheres: why the Sun has a sharp edge and a dark limb

blocks.html: In a plane-parallel atmosphere we measure depth by the vertical optical depth $\tau$ (zero at the top, growing inwards) and directions by $\mu=\cos\theta$. For a grey atmosphere ($\alpha$ independent of $\nu$) with constant flux $F$ and the Eddington approximation $P=U/3$ everywhere, Choudhuri derives

blocks.label: (2.68)-(2.69): the temperature equals T_eff at τ = 2/3.
(2.70) limb-darkening law: at the limb (μ = 0) the intensity is 40 % of the disk centre.

blocks.html: You can see about one optical depth into any gas. At the disk centre your line of sight goes straight down and reaches $\tau=1$ deep, where it is hot. Near the limb you look in obliquely and reach $\tau=1$ (vertical depth $\mu$) much higher up, where it is cooler: the limb is darker and redder. The "surface" of the Sun is just the layer where $\tau\approx2/3$; because opacity rises steeply with depth this layer is only a few hundred km thick, so the edge looks sharp.

Spectral lines: at a line frequency $\alpha_ u$ is larger, so $ au_ u=1$ is reached higher up, where it is cooler, and $S_ u=B_ u(T)$ is smaller: an absorption line. The equivalent width $W$ (the width of a rectangle of zero intensity with the same area as the line) measures line strength. The curve of growth is $W$ against the column density of absorbers: linear when the line is thin, then saturating (flat), then $\propto\sqrt N$ when the damping wings take over.
The curve of growth relates equivalent width and column density (HS24 winter MC9), not perturbation amplitude vs time, not AGN mass vs luminosity.

encounters.title: Energy transport in the interior: diffusion, opacity, convection

blocks.html: Deep inside a star the radiation field is nearly isotropic and the flux is driven by the gradient of radiation pressure, $F=-\frac{c}{\alpha}\frac{dP_{\rm rad}}{dr}$ (with $\alpha=\chi\rho$, $\chi$ the Rosseland mean opacity). With $P_{\rm rad}=\frac13a_BT^4$ and $F=L_r/4\pi r^2$:

blocks.label: Radiative temperature gradient (as given in the HS25 practice exam Q2c).

blocks.html: Opacity laws you need: electron (Thomson) scattering, $\chi_T=n_e\sigma_T/\rho=\sigma_T/m_H=0.04$ m$^2$/kg for ionised hydrogen, independent of $T$ and $\rho$; bound-free and free-free absorption follow Kramers' law $\chi\propto\rho\,T^{-3.5}$.

A photon in the Sun travels only ~1 cm before it is absorbed and re-emitted in a random direction. After $N$ steps of length $l$ it has moved $\sqrt N\,l$. To get out ($R_\odot=7\times10^8$ m) it needs $N=(R/l)^2\sim10^{22}$ steps: a path of $10^{20}$ m, i.e. $10^4$ years or more of travel for a trip light would do in 2 s in vacuum.

When the radiative gradient becomes too steep (high opacity, or huge energy generation in a small core), a rising blob of gas stays hotter and lighter than its surroundings and keeps rising: convection. The Schwarzschild criterion for stability against convection is

blocks.label: Stable (no convection) when the actual temperature gradient is shallower than the adiabatic one.

blocks.html: The Schwarzschild condition as written in the exam ($dT/dr<(1-1/\gamma)(T/P)\,dP/dr$ written with magnitudes of the gradients, HS25 practice MC4) describes material that is stable against convection: energy is then carried by radiation. The Sun is radiative inside $0.7R_\odot$ and convective outside.

encounters.title: Looking through a foggy cloud
encounters.problem: A background source of intensity $I_0$ is seen through a uniform cloud with source function $S=0.3\,I_0$ and optical depth $\tau=2$.

steps.prompt: Fraction of the background that is transmitted, $e^{-\tau}$.
steps.hint: At $\tau=1$ only 37 % gets through; at $\tau=2$ about 14 %.
$I=I_0e^{-\tau}+S(1-e^{-\tau})$. Since $S<I_0$, the cloud darkens the source (absorption).

steps.prompt: Same cloud made very thick ($\tau\to\infty$): intensity in units of $I_0$.

encounters.title: Why air would be opaque if it were ionised (Choudhuri ex. 2.7)
encounters.problem: Fully ionised hydrogen with the density of air, $\rho=1.29$ kg m$^{-3}$. Light is attenuated only by Thomson scattering ($\sigma_T=6.652\times10^{-29}$ m$^2$).

steps.prompt: Path length over which the intensity halves, in m.
steps.hint: $e^{-\alpha L}=1/2\Rightarrow L=\ln2/\alpha\approx14$ m. This is why the Universe became transparent only when electrons were locked into atoms (recombination).

encounters.title: Quick fight: how old is sunlight?
encounters.problem: Photons random-walk out of the Sun with mean free path $l=1/(\chi\rho)$, $\chi\approx0.1$ m$^2$/kg and $\rho\approx10^3$ kg m$^{-3}$ (Choudhuri §2.8). Estimate the escape time in years (within a factor of about 1.3).

steps.hint: $l=1$ cm, $N=(R/l)^2$, path $Nl=R^2/l$, time $R^2/(lc)\approx5\times10^3$ yr (Choudhuri rounds to $10^4$ yr).
